You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

Conflicting rules: one says base = flipud applied to X = [fliplr(I)|I], vertical [f;X;f]; another says 180-rotation first then [B;flip;B]. Session 01a182a6 says: M = hstack(fliplr(A),A); output = vstack(flipud(M), M, flipud(M)). Session 01a18185 says all whole-tile variants FAILED on 5x10 test including 180-rot — but that session ended UNSOLVED. Hmm, but 01a18185 says even 180-rot whole-tile failed; yet 01a1816f solved with 180-rot. Contradiction... maybe 01a18185's constructions were subtly different (e.g., "180-rot whole-tile" meaning different order). The 01a182a6 rule is verified exactly on demo with 0 wrong across multiple sessions. But 01a1816f solved with the 180-rot rule with 0 wrong too... These can't both be right unless inputs were symmetric.

Actually the two rules: rule A: X=[fliplr|I]; out=[flipud(X);X;flipud(X)]. Rule B: Q=180-rot; B=[Q|fliplr(Q)]; out=[B;flipud(B);B]. Note flipud(X) rows = flipud of [fliplr|I]. flipud(X) row i = X[h-1-i] = [fliplr(I)[h-1-i], I[h-1-i]] = [I[h-1-i] reversed? fliplr row stays same reversed row...] Both give out row 0 = reverse of input's last row duplicated. Hmm they may actually be equivalent? flipud(X) vs 180-rot tile: flipud(X) row0 = X[h-1] = [fliplr(I)[h-1] | I[h-1]] = [reverse(I[h-1]) | I[h-1]]. B row0 = [Q[0]|reverse(Q[0])] = [reverse(I[h-1]) | I[h-1]]. Same! And fliplr of flipud(X): [I[h-1] | reverse(I[h-1])]. B is [Q | fliplr(Q)], fliplr(Q)[0] = reverse(Q[0])... wait fliplr(Q) row0 = reverse(Q[0]) = I[h-1]. So B row0 = [reverse(I[h-1]) | I[h-1]] — same. Actually B = [Q | fliplr(Q)]; and X = [fliplr(I)|I]. X row r = [reverse(I[r]) | I[r]]; B row r = [reverse(I[h-1-r]) | I[h-1-r]] = X row h-1-r = flipud(X) row r. So B = flipud(X), and rule B out = [B; flipud(B); B] = [flipud(X); X; flipud(X)] = rule A. They're identical! Great — one consistent rule.

Session 01a18185 failed with all — maybe their constructions had bugs (shape mismatch). Also one session verified on 7x7→21x14 demo exactly. Trust the rule.
